articles.headline: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1
articles.blurb: Project Suncatcher is a moonshot effort by Google to design orbital AI data centers. Its first experimental satellite will launch on October 1. Its aim will be to validate Google's vision for a constellation of AI satellites. The satellite, about the size of a refrigerator, has four custom TPU AI accelerators and solar panels that supply about one kilowatt of power. It will serve as a test of several technologies over its few months of operation.

articles.headline: Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin Is Fueled With $30 Billion of His Fortune
articles.blurb: Jeff Bezos has invested $30 billion in Blue Origin since its founding in 2000. The commitment has helped Blue Origin become a large space company with around 15,000 employees and an ambitious growth plan. Blue Origin recently raised capital from outside investors for the first time. The company expects to produce about $1.4 billion in revenue this year, growing that number to more than $30 billion in 2030.

articles.headline: There's a new way to break RSA that's faster than anything we've seen before
articles.blurb: Researchers have discovered a novel method that uses classical computing to reduce the current RSA security level to an unacceptably low threshold. The practical risk is limited, but still significant. Widely used RSA implementations are also safe. The technology involves signature forgery and reduces the required computing resources by orders of magnitude.

articles.headline: Waymo is scaling fast: Here's what the fleet data shows
articles.blurb: Waymo appears to be concentrating its efforts in just two states. 80% of its roughly 4,000 robotaxis are in California and Texas. Waymo's fleet has grown by nearly half in the past three weeks in Texas. The company's remaining 800 or so vehicles are spread across cities in other states, including Arizona and Florida. A growing number of the vehicles in Waymo's fleet are Chinese-built minivans.

articles.headline: A new trend of CPU shortages
articles.blurb: Many companies are struggling to source CPUs. CPU spot pricing has disappeared because there's no longer any lack of demand for CPUs. It's now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance. Cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don't have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.

articles.headline: Thinking in Systems, Shipping in Loops
articles.blurb: AI has removed the typing from software engineering but left the system design. What's left is designing the loop that decides whether the output is right. Great system design is defined by resilience, self-organization, and hierarchy. Resilience is AI checking its own work, self-organization is the loop learning, and hierarchy is the layering of skills, tools, and sandboxes into composable components that are reused once verified to work.

articles.headline: The Specter Of Neuralese
articles.blurb: Neuralese recurrence is a hypothetical technology that would allow AIs to think dangerous thoughts without getting detected. OpenAI's new Astra model uses a reasoning technique called recurrent depth that makes the model's chain of thought more difficult to monitor by allowing it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models. There is an emerging taboo on creating dangerous neuralese AIs. It is unclear whether OpenAI broke that taboo, as a clear line has yet to be drawn.

articles.headline: Zuckerberg's ‘Tamagotchi-Like' AI Could Be Meta's iPod Moment
articles.blurb: Meta announced a Tamagotchi-like pendant for interacting with its Muse personal agent on Wednesday. The device, expected to be out in time for Christmas, features a customizable character at the center of the screen. It can be worn with a wrist strap, carried in a pocket, or attached to a bag or keychain with a lanyard. The devices can interact with each other when placed near each other. Muse Charm could open up new streams of revenue that could eclipse the company's advertising business.

articles.headline: What it's like to work at an AI-native company
articles.blurb: AI-native company Lovable operates with a flat structure, minimizing traditional titles and meetings, while fostering high autonomy and rapid adaptation. The dynamic environment encourages employees to automate tasks and focus on high-impact, individual contributions, resulting in blurred roles and responsibilities. AI agents, paired with human "agent parents," support daily operations, highlighting the shift towards leveraging AI in company operations.

articles.headline: YC startups are skipping the API and shipping an MCP server
articles.blurb: 36.1% of YC companies with an MCP server have no public API. 36.2% in the 2025 and 2026 batches served an llms.txt. The public API share has barely moved across batches. 81 of the 5,635 reachable YC domains are listed in the official MCP directory.

articles.headline: There are no more moats. You never had one
articles.blurb: Companies are buying more software than ever, but there's no loyalty anymore. They leave the moment something better ships. Migrations are now free, and contracts are monthly. Companies need to have the best product for the week, and then do it again next week. It's no longer about protecting a moat, but going out on the attack.

articles.headline: The SaaStr AI Guide to Building a Top-Tier Inbound AI Agent: 17,000 Conversations, ~600 Meetings Booked, and 60% More New Business
articles.blurb: SaaStr's inbound AI agent conducted 17,000 conversations and booked 600 meetings, boosting new business by 60%. Key improvements included replacing long forms with real-time qualification and direct meeting booking on high-intent pages. The self-serve agent enhanced this by creating personalized, trackable documents and employing heat mapping for deeper insights, supported by a lightweight, custom booking system on their site.

articles.headline: Introducing Amazon CloudWatch Omni: collaborative AI-powered observability for your applications
articles.blurb: Amazon CloudWatch Omni is an AI-powered observability experience for applications and agents. Working in Omni does not require access to the AWS Management Console. The telemetry sent to CloudWatch automatically appears in Omni with no reconfiguration required. Any other workload instrumented with OpenTelemetry sends its telemetry to an OpenTelemetry Protocol endpoint.

articles.headline: Introducing the Image & Video API
articles.blurb: ElevenLabs' Image & Video API allows users to generate images and videos with the same ElevenLabs API used for speech. It supports 18 models, including Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.5, GPT Image 2.5, and Nano Banana Pro. The API is available today on Pro plans and above. Generations cost the same credits as in the ElevenLabs app, and failed generations aren't charged.

articles.headline: Introducing Fast Search in the Perplexity Search API
articles.blurb: Fast Search runs on a Rust-based retrieval and ranking service called Photon that Perplexity built with a small team of engineers and hundreds of agents. It returns 95% of search results in 230 milliseconds or less. Fast Search has a median latency of 160 milliseconds, and it spends less on compute on ranking than Perplexity's default preset. Photon now handles all of the retrieval and ranking across Perplexity, replacing the open-source engine the company was using before.

articles.headline: What it takes to build great products now
articles.blurb: Getting there fast doesn't mean you've built something great. Teams need to decide whether a direction is the best, whether the product fits the team, and whether the product is worth building. The teams answering those questions well are strong in speed, direction, and differentiation. They'll keep moving through the final stretch, weigh many directions before betting on one, and shape the result into something only they would make.

articles.headline: Why Venture Due Diligence Got Worse for Deep Tech
articles.blurb: Venture due diligence for deep tech has worsened, driven by deployment pressure, herding behavior, reliance on lead investors' reputations, and the removal of independent expert review layers. Deals in frontier tech sectors like AI and quantum often close rapidly without thorough technical vetting, exposing investors to unverified risks. Limited partners are advised to mandate independent technical feasibility reviews before deep-tech investments to enhance diligence and protect their capital.

articles.headline: The Most Important Market in AI is the Middle

articles.blurb: This article shows a CSS-only approach to detect overlapping elements with anchor positioning and scroll-driven animations. It uses the result to adapt card layouts without JavaScript, pointing to a new way to build collision-aware interfaces.

articles.headline: A Decision-Only Judge Matches GPT-6 on Routine Evals for 0.36% of the Fee
articles.blurb: CMU tested Jev, a judge that returns only a verdict and label probabilities, against 16 LLM and reward-model judges. It comes within three points of GPT-6 on preference and factuality at 277 times lower fees, though it fails on difficult correctness tasks.

articles.headline: What will make personal AI go big?
articles.blurb: Personal AI needs to feel approachable, earn trust through well-timed permission requests, tackle avoided tasks, and suggest useful next steps. It uses Muse to show why proactive ideas and clear ways to manage ongoing work matter more than generic speed.

articles.headline: A eulogy for the software engineer
articles.blurb: This essay uses the form of a funeral to reckon with AI making implementation work dramatically cheaper. It argues that engineers remain responsible for judgment, clear definitions of done, and passing hard-won taste on to newcomers.

articles.headline: Alchemy (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Alchemy models cloud infrastructure and application logic as a single type-safe Effect program. It supports AWS and Cloudflare resources, while keeping local development, planning, deployment, testing, and CI in one workflow.

articles.headline: Step Code (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Step Code is a terminal coding agent that reads code, makes changes, and runs tests. It supports MCP servers, Agent Skills, plugins, multi-agent orchestration, and longer-running task delegation.

articles.headline: Search (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Search is a small, fast, quiet WebKit browser for macOS with an intentionally minimal interface. It uses the system WebKit engine, which keeps the app small and avoids bundling a second browser engine.

articles.headline: Writing Parquet Files Using Haskell
articles.blurb: This post introduces a Parquet writer in DataHaskell/Dataframe. It centers on the writeParquet function, which takes a dataframe and writes it to Parquet format.

articles.headline: I Opened a Fake Auto Shop for AI Agents
articles.blurb: This experiment creates a fictional garage and sends several AI agents to interact with it. It explores what happens when agents encounter a small business on the open web.

articles.headline: Bringing Private Processing to Meta AI Glasses
articles.blurb: Meta describes using confidential virtual machines and trusted execution environments to run personal-context workloads in the cloud. Remote attestation lets clients verify the code image before sending data, while the design aims to protect memory even from infrastructure operators.

articles.headline: Faster Queries for Debugging Production Agents with Nitro
articles.blurb: Braintrust describes Nitro, which separates storage and compute concurrency and made full-text trace searches more than twice as fast in a production A/B test.

articles.headline: Behind Project Suncatcher, Our Moonshot to Put AI in Space
articles.blurb: Google details its first in-orbit TPU test and the research challenges around radiation, cooling, and satellite interconnects for space-based AI compute.

articles.headline: Manufacturing Trust for AI Agents (Website)
articles.blurb: Docker outlines microVM-based Sandboxes, OCI-based Sandbox Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes as a way to constrain, package, and extend agent work.

articles.headline: Measuring the Back/Forward Cache with Application Metrics
articles.blurb: Sentry explains how its bfcacheMetricsIntegration makes back/forward cache health measurable when ordinary metrics leave cache hits invisible.

articles.headline: How Concurrence governs clinical AI at a trillion-token scale with Unity Gateway
articles.blurb: Concurrence uses Databricks to run and govern clinical AI at an annualized scale of roughly 1.2 trillion input tokens, combining patient data, agent state, testing, evaluations, and access controls on one platform. Unity Gateway centralizes access to approved AI models and tools, helping the company track usage, enforce compliance, and safely scale both clinical and coding agents.

articles.headline: If You Last Used Cassandra 3.11, You Might Not Recognize It Today
articles.blurb: Apache Cassandra 5 loosens many of the constraints teams learned with 3.11, adding storage-attached indexing, unified compaction, native vector search, and built-in repair scheduling. Cassandra 6 goes further with ordered cluster metadata and cross-partition transactions, although partitioning and workload design remain fundamental.

articles.headline: We ported the original Doom to SQL
articles.blurb: CedarDB ported the original Doom's game logic and renderer almost entirely to SQL, running the game loop at its original 35 Hz and rendering at up to 60 FPS. The experiment shows that surprisingly complex real-time logic can work with SQL's set-based model, while database features like transactions, access control, and shared state make multiplayer particularly natural.

articles.headline: Real-time LLM guardrails with Jev: comparing latency and cost
articles.blurb: TypeSafe's Jev uses a purpose-built decision model for real-time AI guardrails, checking agent inputs, responses, and tool calls before they execute. In Arize's tests, it made the same decisions as GPT-5.4 nano while running 15-18x faster and costing 12-14x less per call.

articles.headline: Benchmarks are more broken than we could have imagined
articles.blurb: Horizon audited over 5,000 AI benchmark tasks across 20 datasets and confirmed 29 were broken, with problems including leaked answers, incomplete tests, gameable graders, and failing reference solutions. Many of these flaws actually inflated model scores, highlighting how benchmark results can overstate capabilities when the underlying tasks and graders are unreliable.

articles.headline: DuckDB Now Ships inside dbt v2
articles.blurb: dbt v2's Rust-based Fusion engine now includes a built-in DuckDB adapter, removing the need for a separate adapter installation. It adds DuckLake and Iceberg REST catalog support, writes queryable project metadata as Parquet, and performs SQL analysis that finds type or column problems before warehouse execution. The migration path starts by testing the opt-in v2 parser against existing projects.

articles.headline: Announcing Apache Fluss 1.0: Real-Time Data Foundation for AI
articles.blurb: Apache Fluss 1.0 introduces a stateless Rust HTTP Gateway for metadata, table operations, and batch writes, alongside native Python access and deeper Flink, Spark, Hudi, and Paimon integration. It adds row and log TTLs, predicate pushdown, coordinator high availability, resource protection, and cleanup features, moving the project from incubator-era capabilities toward production real-time lakehouse workloads.

articles.headline: Introducing prompt_jev(): bringing Jev to MotherDuck SQL
articles.blurb: MotherDuck's new prompt_jev function brings Jev directly into SQL, letting users classify and score text at analytics scale without training a model or parsing LLM responses. In its 100,000-row benchmark, Jev achieved 89% accuracy in 40 seconds for $0.50, outperforming the tested LLMs on speed, cost, and accuracy.

articles.headline: Jevflake (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Jevflake brings TypeSafe's Jev decision model into Snowflake through SQL functions and dbt, letting teams classify, score, and ask structured questions about their data with probabilistic answers. It can cache results in dbt models and add tests or human-review queues, making AI classifications reusable parts of normal analytics workflows.

articles.headline: How Adaptive Tail Sampling Works in the OpenTelemetry Collector
articles.blurb: Fixed-rate sampling often discards the rare traces needed in an incident, while ordinary tail sampling loses statistical weights. An adaptive tail sampler for the OpenTelemetry Collector buffers traces, applies ordered rules, and attaches W3C probability thresholds so downstream counts can be reweighted. It adapts by route and service, bounds memory under load, and is progressing upstream toward alpha.

articles.headline: High-Throughput OLTP in Three Simple Steps
articles.blurb: High-throughput transaction systems benefit from co-design rather than copying a connection-pool pattern from a general-purpose database. TigerBeetle models linked transfers atomically, aggregates balances without scans, batches operations automatically while a request is in flight, and prefers time-ordered identifiers for fast idempotency checks. Its benchmark illustrates why batching and ordered IDs can matter more than adding clients.

articles.headline: Profile your Polars queries
articles.blurb: Polars now exposes a query profiler for local open-source workloads.

articles.headline: Host- and Domain-Level Web Graphs July, August, and September 2026
articles.blurb: Common Crawl has released open web graphs covering 245.8 million hosts and 133.2 million domains.

articles.headline: U.S. Soldier Gets 70 Months in Prison for AT&T, Verizon Extortions
articles.blurb: A U.S. Army soldier who pleaded guilty to hacking into multiple telecommunications companies and stealing mobile call and text metadata for more than 100 million AT&T customers in 2024 was sentenced to 70 months in federal prison today and ordered to pay nearly $300,000 in restitution to victims.

articles.headline: Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight
articles.blurb: The consumer data broker Radaris.com has long had a reputation for ignoring requests to remove personal information from its vast empire of people-search services online. That reputation caught up with the company recently in a lawsuit alleging Radaris violated a New Jersey privacy law that provides for hefty fines against data brokers that publish personal information on state law enforcement officials. In the face of repeated stonewalling and prevarication by attorneys for Radaris, the judge in the case ordered that radaris.com and more than a dozen other data broker domains be transferred to the plaintiffs.

articles.headline: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 1,000 Security Holes
articles.blurb: Microsoft Corp. today issued updates to plug at least 974 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, by far its biggest single patch batch ever. Microsoft says artificial intelligence is helping to speed the discovery of vulnerabilities, but security experts warn that many organizations already are struggling to prioritize the more human-intensive endeavor of testing and deploying so many fixes each month.

articles.headline: FBI Probes Service Selling 153M+ Drivers Licenses
articles.blurb: A new identity theft service launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada. Based on interviews with individuals whose licenses are available for purchase on this service, it appears to be siphoning images collected by a widely-used identity verification company based in Louisiana.
